doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Count Basie band and Thad Jones
title: Frank Foster and the flow of ideas
summary: Frank Foster succeeded Thad, writing charts constantly on the bus, which taught Stripling not to be afraid of his own creativity.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Sure, absolutely. Well then Frank came on after Thad. Frank Foster. And had a whole different approach to his way of running the band but it was still a great approach. And he was one of the first people who I saw who had so much music coming out of him. He and Thad, you know we always worry as musicians and artists, like is this just a fluke? Am I going to run out of ideas pretty soon? If you can be around some people like that, I mean Frank would sit on the bus with a pen, P-E-N, and write chart after — it was like he wrote too many charts almost. I’d say, “Frank, we haven’t learned this other one yet.” It’s like he had all this, and it just had to come out. And so you learn by watching people like that, that each of us has this stuff in us. Now if we could just find where it is and what it is. It’s there, you know, and don’t be afraid, like don’t stop it up, and get the cholesterol out and let it just come out. Because we all become so paralyzed with fear. So it’s great to be around people who are, I call them like free spirits. It’s just don’t give a damn, just let it come out. Let your creativity come out, don’t be afraid to be who you are. And it’s like still I’m trying to learn how to do that. I’m trying to learn how to not be me, or try to learn how to not be afraid to be me. It’s like what Tony Bennett once said, if you want to be something really different just try being yourself. It’s that great, just trying to not be afraid of that. And so it’s great to be around creative people like that, to check them out.
